title: Count the calm days
hook: count the days you weren't angry: every day, then every other, then every third (Discourses 2.18)
carry: give the anger nothing to burn

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hexis: habits grow by use. Your line was one ordinary step at a time. Today ends the week.

Days on a language app. Days on this path. Steps on a watch. Streaks are everywhere, and a number going up has a way of keeping people showing up. Miss a day, and it stings a little. The idea is older than it looks. Epictetus gave his students a streak to keep, not for steps or lessons, but for something much harder: the days they got through without losing their temper.
screen: `STREAKS EVERYWHERE.` → `A NUMBER GOING UP.` → `DAYS WITHOUT LOSING YOUR TEMPER.`

segments.voice: It's the same chapter as yesterday, Discourses book two, chapter eighteen, where hexis is formed. If you don't want to be quick-tempered, Epictetus says, then don't feed the habit. Give it nothing that makes it grow. And at first, keep quiet, and count the days you weren't angry. I used to be angry every day. Now every other day. Then every third. Then every fourth. And if you go thirty days, he says, make an offering to God, because the habit is first weakened, and then wiped out. Notice how kind this is. He doesn't say, never get angry again, starting today. He expects relapses. He's measuring the gaps between angry days getting longer. In the same chapter he gives a tool for the moment anger rises. When an impression hits you hard, don't let it carry you off. Say to it: wait for me a little, impression. Let me see what you are, and what you're about. Let me test you. That little pause is how the count goes up. And his very first instruction is easy to miss: keep quiet. Be still at first, and give the anger nothing to burn. The counting grows out of that stillness. The week in a breath: bold outside, sphaira, onoma, astheneia, agōnia, habits grow by use, and now count the calm days.
screen: `DON'T FEED THE HABIT.` · `EVERY DAY, EVERY OTHER, EVERY THIRD.` · `WAIT FOR ME A LITTLE, IMPRESSION.` · `KEEP STILL, THEN COUNT.` · then, large: `COUNT THE CALM DAYS.`

segments.voice: Think back over today, or yesterday if today has barely started, and notice any anger in it, a flash, a slow burn, a sharp word, without judging. If the day was calm, let that be one quiet mark on the count; if it wasn't, no scolding. Then rehearse the pause: picture a hot moment, and hear yourself say, wait a little, let me see what you are.
Orgē. Greek for anger: Epictetus' plan for a quick temper, angry every day, then every other, then every third, until thirty calm days in a row.
Your line: give the anger nothing to burn. Every other day is progress too. Another week, done.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a private tally of days without anger, expecting setbacks and watching the gaps between angry days grow.
